NoteKey Takeaways




Mixed-effects models combine fixed effects, describing average relationships, with random effects, describing variation between groups. The approach is useful when observations are grouped, including repeated measurements for the same participants over time. As such, a group can be a set of observations belonging to one individual, these data are grouped.
Repeated observations help distinguish variability between participants from variability within participants. The estimation of these are possible using mixed-effects modelling.
The conditional growth model is a backbone of much of research in medicine and biology. The model incorporates an interaction between time and the intervention to describe how the intervention effect changes over time.

ID identifies the herd, TIME records the measurement time in months, and DV is the dependent variable (milk fat content).
We might expect milk fat content to increase over time while differing between herds at the same time point. The question is how to represent those differences in a model.



Figure 4.1 Longitudinal milk fat data in five herds.


The above plot contains one trajectory per herd. Variation in the starting values represents between-herd differences in intercepts, while variation in the rate of change represents between-herd differences in slopes.
We have a few potential approaches for modelling these data. I will go through these belows along with their positives and negatives.

title: Part Four
text:
Naïve Pooling
One approach is to fit a single regression line through all observations:
\[
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1t_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where \(i\) identifies a herd and \(j\) identifies an observation within that herd.
This model ignores herd groups. All differences between observations and the common regression line are assigned to the residual error term of the model, including persistent differences between herds.
Naïve pooling treats the observations as independent even when the study design gives reasons to expect dependence. Ignoring grouping does not always change the estimated average slope substantially. However, it can affect its standard error, confidence interval and p-value. More importantly, the naïve pool approach leaves the between-herd variation as undescribed residual noise while the data violates the assumption on independence of errors.

title: Part Four
text:
Complete Pooling
Another approach is to average the observations at each time point and fit a regression to those averages:

herd_means <- aggregate(DV ~ TIME, data = herd_dat, FUN = mean)
m_herd_means <- lm(DV ~ TIME, data = herd_means)
summary(m_herd_means)

Aggregation can be useful when the mean trajectory is the object of interest. However, we are discarding information on variability. Time-point averages calculated from the same herds can also remain correlated. Averaging does not automatically make them independent.
An especially smooth mean trajectory can produce a very small regression residual standard deviation. That value describes deviations of the averages from the fitted line. It should not be interpreted as the variation among individual observations or as a complete description of uncertainty in the original data.
Aggregation also changes the level of the analysis. Associations between group averages need not equal associations between individuals. Inferring an individual relationship from an aggregate relationship is known as the ecological fallacy.

title: Part Four
text:
No Pooling
We can instead estimate a separate intercept for each herd:
\[
Y_{ij}=\alpha_i+\beta_1t_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}.
\]

m_herd_id <- lm(DV ~ TIME + ID - 1, data = herd_dat)
summary(m_herd_id)

The - 1 removes the overall intercept. R then estimates a coefficient for each herd intercept, rather than an intercept for a reference herd and differences from that reference.
These models can describe the observed herds well. However, they do not specify a population distribution for the herd coefficients. A coefficient for a new herd is therefore not inferred from this parameterisation. Estimating many separate coefficients can also become difficult if some groups have few observations.

title: Part Four
text:
Partial Pooling
A mixed-effects model represents the herd coefficients as deviations from population coefficients:
\[
Y_{ij}=(\beta_0+b_{0i})+(\beta_1+b_{1i})t_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}.
\]
Here, \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are the fixed effects. They describe the population intercept and slope. The random effects, \(b_{0i}\) and \(b_{1i}\), describe the deviations for herd \(i\).
For a conventional linear mixed-effects model, we assume:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0i}\\b_{1i}\end{pmatrix}
\sim N\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \tau_{01}\\
\tau_{01} & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix}
\right),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
The variance \(\tau_0^2\) describes variation in intercepts between herds, \(\tau_1^2\) describes variation in slopes, and \(\tau_{01}\) describes their covariance. The residual variance \(\sigma^2\) describes variation remaining around each herd’s trajectory. We assume that different herds are independent and that the residuals are independent conditional on the model’s random effects.
The model estimates the fixed effects and variance components. It also predicts each herd’s random effects using both its observations and the population distribution. This “partial pooling” allows groups to share information.
For a simple random-intercept model with a known common mean, equal residual variance, and \(n_i\) observations in group \(i\), the idea can be illustrated by:
\[
\widehat{\alpha}_i\approx
w_i\bar y_i+(1-w_i)\widehat\beta_0,
\qquad
w_i=\frac{\tau_0^2}{\tau_0^2+\sigma^2/n_i}.
\]
The group estimate lies between its observed mean and the estimated population mean. A group with many precise observations receives a larger weight on its own data. Greater residual noise or fewer observations leads to stronger shrinkage towards the population mean. The weights are more complicated for models with predictors and random slopes, but the principle is the same.

title: Part Four
section: Fitting a Mixed-Effects Model in R
text:
Fitting a Mixed-Effects Model in R
The lmer() function in R fits linear mixed-effects models. The term before the vertical bar specifies the random coefficients, and the term after it specifies the grouping variable.

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

m_herd_mixed <- lmerTest::lmer(
  DV ~ TIME + (1 + TIME | ID),
  data = herd_dat,
  REML = TRUE
)

summary(m_herd_mixed)
fixef(m_herd_mixed)
VarCorr(m_herd_mixed)
ranef(m_herd_mixed)
coef(m_herd_mixed)
isSingular(m_herd_mixed)

TIME gives the fixed time slope. (1 + TIME | ID) allows the intercept and time slope to vary between herds and estimates their correlation. The overall intercept is included by default. lmerTest supplies approximate fixed-effect tests, using Satterthwaite degrees of freedom by default.
The output distinguishes several quantities:







Output
Interpretation




Fixed-effect estimate
Estimated population coefficient


Fixed-effect standard error
Uncertainty in that estimated coefficient


Random-effect standard deviation
Estimated variation in the coefficient between groups


Random-effect correlation
Association between the groups’ intercept and slope deviations


Residual standard deviation
Remaining variation around the conditional fitted values


Correlation of fixed effects
Correlation between coefficient estimators, rather than between individual random effects



A random-effect standard deviation is not the standard error of the fixed effect. We can estimate the population mean precisely while individuals still vary substantially around it.

title: Part Four
text:
Repeated-Measures ANOVA
Repeated-measures ANOVA also accounts for repeated observations. It usually treats measurement occasions as categories and requires complete records.
Mixed-effects models provide more flexibility for unequal observation schedules, continuous time, and differing numbers of measurements per participant. They can also use available outcome observations under appropriate assumptions about missingness. However, we still need a suitable mean model and covariance structure. Choosing a mixed-effects model does not remove those requirements.

title: Part Four
text:
Fixed Effects and Random Effects
The terminology can be confusing. A fixed effect is a coefficient shared across the population, while a random effect is a group-specific deviation modelled as a draw from a distribution.
In the lecture video, we take a look at an association between smoking and an inflammation biomarker. For independent observations, we could write:
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{Smoking}_i+\varepsilon_i,
\]
Where smoking is coded zero or one. The coefficient \(\beta_1\) is the difference in expected inflammation between smokers and nonsmokers.
Now consider an observational follow-up in which we measure the same people before and after they begin smoking. Their measurements are paired. A random intercept can represent persistent differences in baseline inflammation:
\[
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{Smoking}_{ij}+b_{0i}+\varepsilon_{ij}.
\]
We can now distinguish variation between participants from variation around each participant’s predicted response. The model recognises that observations from one person share the same \(b_{0i}\).

title: Part Four
text:
Association and Causality
A statistically significant coefficient does not establish that changing the predictor would cause the estimated change in the outcome (counterfactual interpretation). Confounding, selection and the timing of observations matter.
The Bradford Hill considerations discussed in the lecture include strength and consistency of association, specificity, temporality, a biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experimental evidence and analogy. They help organise reasoning about evidence. These are not a checklist that defines causality but it does give.a good indication of some of the factors that allow us to distinquish between associations and causality. What are the implications here? Well, it turns out that time-series data is critical for determinating causality. Therefore, the mixed-effects methods are super relevant.
Randomisation provides a different form of evidence by making treatment assignment independent of participant characteristics in expectation. It does not guarantee exact balance in a realised sample. Fisher’s lady-tasting-tea example illustrates how a randomised experiment can compare an observed result with what chance alone would produce.

title: Part Four
text:
Cross-Sectional and Real-World Data
A cross-sectional study observes a population at one time or over a short interval. It can describe prevalence and associations, but often provides limited information about the sequence of events.
Even without repeated observations for each person, patients may be grouped by hospital. A model such as:

hospital_model <- lmerTest::lmer(
  inflammation ~ treatment + age + (1 | Hospital),
  data = hospital_data
)

This allows hospital baselines to vary randomly.
With repeated measurements of patients within hospitals, a nested structure could be written as (1 | Hospital/ID). This expands into a hospital intercept and an intercept for each hospital–patient combination. The grouping structure should reflect how the observations were collected.
Retrospective healthcare data may contain irregular measurement times and unequal numbers of observations. Mixed-effects models can represent that structure.

title: Part Four
text:
Preparing the Predictors
As in Part Two, examine variable definitions, units, distributions and missingness before fitting a model. Consider whether time zero is meaningful and whether a linear time effect is plausible over the observed period.
Highly correlated predictors can make individual coefficients difficult to estimate. Regression does not require predictors to be mutually independent. The problem is that closely related predictors supply little independent information about their separate coefficients.
Centring a predictor changes the interpretation of the intercept:
\[
x_{ij}^{c}=x_{ij}-c.
\]
If \(c\) is baseline time, the intercept refers to baseline. If \(c\) is the mean, it refers to the mean predictor value, conditional on the other predictors. Standardising additionally divides by a standard deviation. The corresponding coefficient then describes a one-standard-deviation change.
For longitudinal predictors, distinguish changes within a person from differences between people. An individual’s mean predictor value and their deviation from that mean can have different associations with the outcome. A random intercept alone does not guarantee that one common slope isolates a within-person effect.

title: Part Four
text:
Choosing Model Terms
Include predictors because they help answer the research question or describe the process generating the data. Important adjustment variables may remain relevant even when their individual p-values are large. Interactions arbe best considered using a scientific or design-based rationale.
An unexpected coefficient sign is a reason to investigate coding, confounding, collinearity and model form. Removing a variable simply because its sign conflicts with an expectation can hide an important feature of the data. Retaining unnecessary predictors can also reduce precision, particularly in small datasets.
Choose the random-effects structure alongside the fixed effects. For repeated observations over time, a random slope may be appropriate if individuals plausibly change at different rates and the observation schedule supplies enough information to estimate that variation.

title: Part Four
text:
The Thyroid Hormone-Level Example
The lecture uses a simulated treatment example with substantial differences in baseline hormone levels between participants. We will use an illustrative dataset in which each of 50 participants contributes five observations under each of two conditions. This makes the treatment indicator vary within participants and permits comparison with a model containing separate participant intercepts.
The design is an educational illustration. It does not establish that treatment and control periods would be exchangeable in a clinical study. A real before-and-after or crossover analysis would also consider period effects and, where relevant, carryover.

set.seed(403)

n_patients <- 50
exdata <- expand.grid(
  OBS = 1:5,
  IV = 0:1,
  ID = seq_len(n_patients)
)

patient_baseline <- rnorm(n_patients, mean = 36, sd = 11)
exdata$DV <- patient_baseline[exdata$ID] +
  10 * exdata$IV +
  rnorm(nrow(exdata), mean = 0, sd = 3.2)
exdata$ID <- factor(exdata$ID)

# Randomly remove 18% of outcome values, leaving identifiers intact.
missing_rows <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(exdata)),
  size = round(0.18 * nrow(exdata))
)
exdata$DV[missing_rows] <- NA_real_

mean(is.na(exdata$DV))
library(naniar)
vis_miss(exdata)

boxplot(DV ~ ID, data = exdata,
        xlab = "Participant", ylab = "Hormone level (illustrative units)")
boxplot(DV ~ IV, data = exdata,
        xlab = "Condition: 0 = control, 1 = treatment", ylab = "Hormone level")
boxplot(DV ~ OBS + IV, data = exdata,
        xlab = "Observation and condition", ylab = "Hormone level")

The simulated effect is constant over the measurement occasions. Differences between participant baselines are much larger than the residual noise.

title: Part Four
text:
Comparing Pooling Approaches
We first restrict all models to the same complete rows:

analysis_dat <- exdata[complete.cases(exdata[c("DV", "IV", "ID")]), ]

m_pool <- lm(DV ~ IV, data = analysis_dat)
m_id <- lm(DV ~ IV + ID - 1, data = analysis_dat)

m_null <- lmerTest::lmer(
  DV ~ 1 + (1 | ID), data = analysis_dat, REML = TRUE
)
m_treat <- lmerTest::lmer(
  DV ~ IV + (1 | ID), data = analysis_dat, REML = TRUE
)

summary(m_pool)
summary(m_id)
summary(m_null)
summary(m_treat)

The pooled model places baseline differences between patients into its residual error. The model with fixed participant intercepts estimates each baseline separately. The mixed-effects model estimates a population baseline and a distribution of deviations around it.
Here, treatment varies within each participant. If treatment were constant within each participant in a parallel-arm study, its coefficient would be collinear with a full set of fixed participant indicators in m_id. That model could not estimate the treatment effect separately. A random-intercept model makes a different assumption and can estimate a between-participant treatment association, subject to the study design and its assumptions.

title: Part Four
text:
Interpreting the Model Output
The model output for the treatment mixed-effects model reports approximately:



Quantity
Slide estimate




Fixed intercept
36.45


Fixed treatment coefficient
10.04


Between-participant intercept standard deviation
11.06


Residual standard deviation
3.19



The intercept represents the expected outcome under control. Treatment is associated with an increase of about 10 units. Participants vary around the population intercept, with a standard deviation of about 11 units. Their individual observations vary around the conditional model predictions, with a residual standard deviation of about 3.2 units.
jtools::summ() provides an alternative summary:

jtools::summ(m_treat)

The marginal \(R^2\) summarises variation accounted for by the fixed effects, while the conditional \(R^2\) includes the random effects. A much higher conditional \(R^2\) indicates that the grouping structure accounts for considerable variation. A high conditional \(R^2\) does not by itself demonstrate accurate predictions for new participants whose random effects are unknown.
For a random-intercept model, the intraclass correlation coefficient is:
\[
\operatorname{ICC}=\frac{\tau_0^2}{\tau_0^2+\sigma^2}.
\]
Using the variances gives \(122.4/(122.4+10.2)\approx0.92\). Conditional on the fixed predictors, this is the correlation implied for two observations from the same participant. It describes the proportion of remaining variance associated with differences between participants. With random slopes, the implied correlations also depend on predictor values.

title: Part Four
text:
Population and Individual Predictions
A population prediction uses only the fixed effects. A conditional (e.g., individual) prediction also uses the estimated random effect for an observed participant:

analysis_dat$population_pred <- predict(m_treat, re.form = NA)
analysis_dat$individual_pred <- predict(m_treat, re.form = NULL)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(analysis_dat$population_pred, analysis_dat$DV,
     xlab = "Population prediction", ylab = "Observed outcome")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
plot(analysis_dat$individual_pred, analysis_dat$DV,
     xlab = "Individual prediction", ylab = "Observed outcome")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Individual predictions usually fit the existing observations more closely because they use information about each participant. That is a different prediction task from predicting a new participant.

title: Part Four
text:
Residual Diagnostics and Model Stability
Examine residuals against fitted values, time, treatment and other important predictors. Look for systematic trends and changes in spread. A QQ plot helps assess whether the conditional residual distribution is reasonably compatible with a normal distribution.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fitted(m_treat), resid(m_treat),
     xlab = "Conditional fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(resid(m_treat))
qqline(resid(m_treat))
boxplot(resid(m_treat) ~ analysis_dat$IV,
        xlab = "Condition", ylab = "Residual")
plot(analysis_dat$OBS, resid(m_treat),
     xlab = "Observation occasion", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

isSingular(m_treat)
VarCorr(m_treat)

Random effects also have distributional assumptions, although their predicted values are shrunken and should not be treated as independent raw observations for a normality test. Serial patterns remaining within participants can indicate residual autocorrelation that the random intercept does not capture.
A singular fit means that an estimated random-effects covariance matrix has reduced rank. A variance near zero or an intercept–slope correlation near \(-1\) or \(1\) can indicate this. Consider whether the design supports the proposed random-effects structure before changing optimiser settings or removing terms.
Validation should reflect the intended prediction task. To assess predictions for new patients, hold out entire patients. Randomly splitting rows can place observations from the same patient in both the training and test sets and give an optimistic assessment.

title: Part Four
text:
Likelihood-Ratio Tests and Information Criteria
For nested models fitted by ML to the same observations, the likelihood-ratio statistic is:
\[
D=2\left[\ell(\widehat\theta_{\text{full}})
-\ell(\widehat\theta_{\text{reduced}})\right].
\]
Under suitable conditions, this is approximately chi-squared distributed with degrees of freedom equal to the number of additional parameters. We can test the addition of treatment while retaining the random-intercept structure:

m_null_ml <- update(m_null, REML = FALSE)
m_treat_ml <- update(m_treat, REML = FALSE)
anova(m_null_ml, m_treat_ml)

AIC(m_null_ml, m_treat_ml)
BIC(m_null_ml, m_treat_ml)

A small P-value indicates evidence against the reduced model under the test assumptions. It does not quantify clinical importance. Tests that add or remove variance components require extra care because a variance of zero is on the boundary of its allowed values, and the usual chi-squared reference distribution may not apply.
The general information-criterion formulas are:
\[
\operatorname{AIC}=-2\ell(\widehat\theta)+2k,
\qquad
\operatorname{BIC}=-2\ell(\widehat\theta)+k\log(n),
\]
where \(k\) counts the estimated model parameters, including relevant variance and covariance parameters. Lower values indicate a better balance between fit and the corresponding complexity penalty among the models compared. The usual BIC penalty exceeds the AIC penalty when \(n>e^2\). These criteria are relative measures, and comparisons require compatible likelihoods and the same response observations.

title: Part Four
text:
Displaying Effects and Confidence Intervals
Predicted means and their uncertainty often communicate an effect more clearly than a coefficient table:

library(effects)
plot(allEffects(m_treat))

We can use a parametric bootstrap to calculate confidence intervals for the fixed effects:

set.seed(404)
confint(
  m_treat,
  parm = "beta_",
  method = "boot",
  nsim = 1000,
  boot.type = "perc"
)

This simulates datasets from the fitted mixed-effects model and refits it, rather than resampling individual rows as if they were independent. Inspect warnings and failed fits. For a nonparametric bootstrap of grouped data, the resampling scheme must also preserve the relevant dependence, for example by resampling participants as whole groups.

title: Part Four
text:
The Likelihood Function
For independent observations with density or probability mass function \(f(y_i\mid\theta)\), the likelihood is:
\[
L(\theta\mid\mathbf y)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}f(y_i\mid\theta).
\]
The observed data are held fixed while we vary the candidate parameter values. For continuous data, the factors are probability densities, rather than probabilities of observing an exact value. The likelihood is not a probability distribution for the parameters.
We commonly maximise the log likelihood:
\[
\ell(\theta)=\log L(\theta\mid\mathbf y)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log f(y_i\mid\theta).
\]
Equivalently, an optimiser may minimise the negative log likelihood. In a mixed-effects model, the marginal likelihood accounts for the random-effects distribution. Observations from one participant are not treated as marginally independent.

title: Part Four
section: Estimating a Normal Mean and Variance
text:
Estimating a Normal Mean and Variance
For independent observations from \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the log likelihood is:
\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2)
=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
The ML estimates are:
\[
\widehat\mu=\bar y,
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{ML}}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)^2.
\]
We use the data to estimate the mean and then measure deviations from that estimated mean. The variance estimate therefore tends to be too small:
\[
E\left(\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{ML}}\right)
=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2.
\]
The familiar sample variance uses \(n-1\) in the denominator to correct this bias. This is a useful starting point for understanding REML.

title: Part Four
text:
Restricted or Residual Maximum Likelihood
REML estimates variance components while accounting for estimation of the fixed effects. In an ordinary normal linear model with \(p\) fixed-effect coefficients, including the intercept, the analogous variance estimates are:
\[
\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n},
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{REML}}=\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-p}.
\]
Mixed-effects models have a more complex covariance structure, so REML is not generally implemented by replacing one denominator. The underlying motivation remains to reduce bias in variance-component estimation arising from estimation of the mean structure.
The ordinary normal-model example shows downward ML variance bias. Small datasets can produce unstable estimates in either direction in an individual fit, but that is different from the systematic bias illustrated above. REML does not guarantee precise or unbiased estimates of every variance component in every mixed-effects model.

title: Part Four
section: When to Use ML and REML
text:
When to Use ML and REML
For lmer(), REML is the default. Set the argument explicitly when comparing models:

# ML for comparing models with different fixed effects.
m_comparison <- lmerTest::lmer(
  DV ~ IV + (1 | ID), data = analysis_dat, REML = FALSE
)

# REML for estimating the selected model.
m_final <- update(m_comparison, REML = TRUE)
summary(m_final)

REML likelihoods based on different fixed-effect structures are not directly comparable. Use ML when comparing models that add or remove fixed effects, including AIC comparisons. After selecting a model, a common approach is to refit it using REML.
Models with the same fixed-effect structure can sometimes be compared using REML to investigate different covariance structures. That requires a suitable comparison method and attention to boundary issues. The restriction is therefore more specific than saying that REML can never be used for model comparison.

title: Part Four
text:
A Paediatric Diet Example
Suppose we follow children receiving a control diet or an intervention diet. Each child belongs to one group and has repeated measurements of body weight. Children may differ in baseline weight and growth rate.
A spaghetti plot, with one line per child, shows individual trajectories. If the group trajectories increasingly separate, a time-by-diet interaction may describe that pattern.
The lecture discusses follow-up over two years. For the illustrative code below, we use 100 children measured at four occasions, producing 400 observations, matching the number of observations in the slide model output. The chosen schedule is illustrative.

set.seed(405)

n_children <- 100
dietdata <- expand.grid(
  Months = c(0, 6, 12, 24),
  ID = seq_len(n_children)
)
diet_assignment <- sample(rep(0:1, each = n_children / 2))
dietdata$Diet <- diet_assignment[dietdata$ID]

child_intercepts <- rnorm(n_children, mean = 0, sd = 0.94)
child_slopes <- rnorm(n_children, mean = 0, sd = 0.075)

dietdata$BW <- 24.8 + child_intercepts[dietdata$ID] +
  0.14 * dietdata$Diet +
  (0.25 + child_slopes[dietdata$ID]) * dietdata$Months +
  0.25 * dietdata$Diet * dietdata$Months +
  rnorm(nrow(dietdata), mean = 0, sd = 0.44)
dietdata$ID <- factor(dietdata$ID)

plot(BW ~ Months, data = dietdata, type = "n",
     xlab = "Months", ylab = "Body weight (kg)")
for (id in levels(dietdata$ID)) {
  one_child <- dietdata[dietdata$ID == id, ]
  one_child <- one_child[order(one_child$Months), ]
  lines(one_child$Months, one_child$BW,
        col = if (one_child$Diet[1] == 0) "orange" else "steelblue")
}
legend("topleft", legend = c("Control", "Intervention"),
       col = c("orange", "steelblue"), lty = 1, bty = "n")

The coefficients specify an illustrative growth pattern and should not be interpreted as evidence about a particular dietary intervention.

title: Part Four
text:
A Conditional Growth Model
We can write:
\[
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+b_{0i}
+\beta_1t_{ij}+b_{1i}t_{ij}
+\beta_2\operatorname{Diet}_i
+\beta_3t_{ij}\operatorname{Diet}_i
+\varepsilon_{ij}.
\]
The fixed effects describe average growth and the difference between diets. The random intercept and slope describe variation between children within those average patterns.

m_growth <- lmerTest::lmer(
  BW ~ Months * Diet + (1 + Months | ID),
  data = dietdata,
  REML = TRUE
)
summary(m_growth)
VarCorr(m_growth)
isSingular(m_growth)

In an R formula, Months * Diet expands to Months + Diet + Months:Diet. The random-effect term estimates intercept variation, time-slope variation and their covariance. (Months | ID) also includes a random intercept by default, so it is equivalent to (1 + Months | ID).
Diet is constant within each child. A random time slope is identifiable from repeated time observations, whereas a random diet slope within child would not have the same interpretation or information available in this design.

title: Part Four
text:
Interpreting the Interaction
With control coded zero and intervention coded one, the fixed-effect trajectories are:
\[
E(Y\mid t,\operatorname{Diet}=0)=\beta_0+\beta_1t,
\]
\[
E(Y\mid t,\operatorname{Diet}=1)
=(\beta_0+\beta_2)+(\beta_1+\beta_3)t.
\]
The intervention-minus-control difference at time \(t\) is:
\[
\Delta(t)=\beta_2+\beta_3t.
\]
The slide model reports approximately \(\beta_0=24.80\), \(\beta_1=0.247\), \(\beta_2=0.144\) and \(\beta_3=0.254\). The interpretation is:







Coefficient
Meaning




Intercept
Expected baseline weight in the control group, about 24.80 kg


Months
Average control-group growth, about 0.247 kg per month


Diet
Intervention-minus-control baseline difference, about 0.144 kg


Months: Diet
Difference in growth rates, about 0.254 kg per month



The intervention-group growth rate is approximately \(0.247+0.254=0.501\) kg per month. At 12 months, the modelled difference is approximately \(0.144+12(0.254)=3.19\) kg.
A nonsignificant diet main effect refers to the difference at time zero. It does not imply that the diet groups follow the same trajectory. The interaction addresses a different hypothesis: whether their average growth rates differ.
If we centre time at 12 months, the diet main effect becomes the difference at 12 months. The fitted trajectories remain the same. Interpret main effects at the reference value of the interacting predictor.

title: Part Four
section: Testing and Displaying Different Growth Rates
text:
Testing and Displaying Different Growth Rates
To test the interaction, compare models with the same random-effects structure and use ML:

m_growth_additive <- lmerTest::lmer(
  BW ~ Months + Diet + (1 + Months | ID),
  data = dietdata, REML = FALSE
)
m_growth_interaction <- update(
  m_growth_additive, . ~ . + Months:Diet
)
anova(m_growth_additive, m_growth_interaction)

plot(effects::allEffects(m_growth))
plot(m_growth)
qqnorm(resid(m_growth))
qqline(resid(m_growth))

The uncertainty in the estimated difference at a selected time depends on both coefficient variances and their covariance:
\[
\operatorname{Var}\{\widehat\Delta(t)\}
=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_2)
+t^2\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_3)
+2t\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_2,\widehat\beta_3).
\]
Adding the two standard errors would not give the correct standard error of the time-specific difference.
Check whether linear growth adequately describes the observed interval. A random slope accommodates variation in linear growth rates, but does not itself describe curvature. We may need a nonlinear time term or another mean function if the trajectories change shape.

title: Part Three
text:
NoteKey Takeaways




Here I introduce generalised linear models (GLMs). GLMs extend linear regression to dependent variables of other types than continuous data.
A GLM combines a random component, describing the distribution of the dependent variable; a systematic component, consisting of the linear predictor; and a link function connecting the expected response to the linear predictor.
Logistic regression can be used to model binary outcomes, where the inverse-logit function transforms predictions to probabilities between zero and one. The model coefficients are expressed on the log-odds scale.
Poisson regression is used to model count data. Important considerations include overdispersion and zero-inflation, which may require another model such as negative binomial or zero-inflated regression.
Ordinal logistic regression can be used for ordered categorical outcomes. While, unordered categorical data can be modelled using binomial probit or multinomial probit regression.
Survival analysis concerns the time until an event, accounting for right censoring (survival beyond the study period). Kaplan-Meier curves describe survival over time, while Cox regression estimates associations between predictors and the hazard of an event.

title: Part Three
section: What is a Generalised Linear Model?
text:
What is a Generalised Linear Model?
A generalised linear model has three main components:

A Random component: the dependent variable \(Y\) follows a probability distribution from the exponential family, with a mean \(\mu\).
A Systematic component: a linear predictor combines the predictors and regression coefficients.
A Link function: a mathematical function connects the expected value of the dependent variable to the linear predictor.

The linear predictor can be written as:
\[
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\beta_2x_{i2}+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ik}
=\mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol{\beta}.
\]
The link function, \(g(\cdot)\), connects the mean response \(\mu_i=E(Y_i)\) to this linear predictor:
\[
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i.
\]
We can then transform the prediction back to the original scale of the dependent variable using the inverse link function:
\[
\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i).
\]
The link function makes it possible to model a response that does not itself have a linear relationship with the predictors. For example, probabilities must remain between zero and one, while expected counts cannot be negative. An appropriate link function transforms these expected responses to a scale on which they can be modelled using a linear predictor.
The regression coefficients are usually estimated using maximum likelihood estimation. We therefore choose the coefficients that make the observed data most likely under the selected probability distribution and model.

title: Part Three
text:
Linear Regression as a GLM
An ordinary linear regression is a special case of the generalised linear model. We assume that the dependent variable is normally distributed around its expected value:
\[
Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma^2).
\]
The identity link is used:
\[
g(\mu_i)=\mu_i=\eta_i.
\]
Because the link function does not transform the mean, the expected response is directly equal to the linear predictor:
\[
\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ik}.
\]
The residual standard deviation, \(\sigma\), is estimated from the data. As we saw in Part Two, an ordinary linear regression can be estimated by least squares. Under the assumption of normally distributed errors, this gives the same coefficient estimates as maximum likelihood estimation.
Other combinations of distributions and link functions allow us to model different kinds of dependent variables. Common examples include:

Binary outcomes: binomial distribution with a logit link.
Count outcomes: Poisson distribution with a log link.
Positive continuous outcomes: gamma distribution, commonly with a log or inverse link.
Ordered categorical outcomes: an ordinal model, commonly using a logit link.

The general modelling procedure is therefore:

Specify the distribution of the dependent variable.
Specify a vector or matrix of predictors.
Use a link function to connect the expected response to the linear predictor.
Estimate the regression coefficients, usually using maximum likelihood estimation.
Use the inverse link function to predict the dependent variable on its original scale.
Assess the model fit and residual errors using diagnostics suited to the selected model.

In the following sections, we will look at logistic regression, Poisson regression and ordered categorical regression. We will also briefly consider how unordered categorical outcomes can be modelled.

title: Part Three
text:
Modelling Binary Outcomes
Suppose that disease status \(Y_i\) is coded as one when disease is present and zero when it is absent. We can describe the outcome using a Bernoulli distribution:
\[
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),
\]
where \(p_i\) is the probability that disease is present for observation \(i\).
If we fitted a conventional linear regression directly to the binary response, its predictions would not necessarily remain between zero and one. Logistic regression resolves this by using the logit link:
\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_i)
=\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ik}.
\]
The inverse-logit function transforms the linear predictor back into a probability:
\[
p_i=\frac{\exp(\eta_i)}{1+\exp(\eta_i)}
=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-\eta_i)}.
\]
This nonlinear transformation bounds the model predictions between zero and one. The fitted probabilities can then be mapped to the observed binary outcomes.

title: Part Three
section: An Example of Logistic Regression in R
text:
An Example of Logistic Regression in R
In the example presented in the slides, disease status is modelled as a function of a continuous biomarker, x1:

m1_binom <- glm(
  y ~ x1,
  family = "binomial",
  data = binom_dat
)

summary(m1_binom)

The model can be written as:
\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}.
\]
The output is similar to the output from an ordinary linear regression. It includes the coefficient estimates, standard errors, test statistics and P-values. The standard errors indicate the uncertainty in our estimates of the model coefficients.
Because the outcome is discrete, it does not make sense to summarise model fit using the residual standard deviation in the same way as for ordinary linear regression. The output instead includes the null deviance and residual deviance.
The null deviance describes the error from a model containing only an intercept. The residual deviance describes the error remaining after the predictor or predictors have been included. A lower deviance indicates better fit to the observed data. In the example, the null deviance is approximately 130.7 and the residual deviance is approximately 92.0, representing a substantial decrease after including the biomarker.
For nested models, the difference in deviance can be assessed using a likelihood-ratio test. Under the null hypothesis, the decrease in deviance is approximately chi-squared distributed, with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in the number of estimated parameters. Adding one uninformative parameter would, on average, reduce the deviance by approximately one. A substantially larger decrease indicates that the added parameter may improve the model beyond what would be expected by chance.
The output also includes the Akaike information criterion (AIC). AIC is mainly useful when comparing candidate models fitted to the same outcome data. Lower values indicate a better trade-off between model fit and complexity; the value is not particularly meaningful on its own.

title: Part Three
text:
Interpreting Logistic Regression Coefficients
Logistic regression coefficients can be difficult to interpret directly because they describe changes in the log odds rather than constant changes in probability. The relationship between the linear predictor and the probability is nonlinear. A given change in the linear predictor has its largest effect on probability near \(p=0.5\) and a smaller effect near zero or one.
One straightforward approach is to calculate predicted probabilities at meaningful predictor values. For example, we can calculate the probability at the mean biomarker value and then calculate how this probability changes when the biomarker increases by one unit:

library(arm)

p_mean <- invlogit(
  coef(m1_binom)[1] +
    coef(m1_binom)[2] * mean(binom_dat$x1)
)

p_x1 <- invlogit(coef(m1_binom)[1] + coef(m1_binom)[2] * 1)
p_x2 <- invlogit(coef(m1_binom)[1] + coef(m1_binom)[2] * 2)

p_difference <- p_x2 - p_x1

The resulting probability difference depends on where we are on the logistic curve. We should therefore calculate effects over values of the predictors that are relevant to the research question.

The Divide-by-Four Rule
The logistic curve is steepest at its centre, where \(p=0.5\). At this point, the slope of the inverse-logit curve with respect to a continuous predictor is:
\[
\frac{\beta_j}{4}.
\]
Consequently, \(\beta_j/4\) gives an approximate upper bound for the change in probability associated with a one-unit increase in \(x_j\), holding the other predictors constant (Gelman and Hill (2007)). In the slide example, a coefficient of approximately 1.8 gives a maximum probability difference of approximately 0.45.
This is a useful approximation, but it is not the probability change at every predictor value. Calculating predicted probabilities is generally clearer.


Odds Ratios
If an outcome has probability \(p\), its odds are:
\[
\operatorname{odds}=\frac{p}{1-p}.
\]
An odds of one corresponds to a probability of 0.5. Exponentiating a logistic regression coefficient gives an odds ratio:
\[
OR_j=\exp(\beta_j).
\]
For a continuous predictor, this is the multiplicative change in the odds associated with a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding the other predictors constant. Odds ratios should not be interpreted as risk ratios, particularly when the outcome is common.

title: Part Three
text:
Prediction
We can use predict() to calculate fitted probabilities over a sequence of biomarker values:

dat_new <- data.frame(
  x1 = seq(
    from = min(binom_dat$x1),
    to = max(binom_dat$x1),
    length.out = 100
  )
)

dat_new$Predicted <- predict(
  m1_binom,
  type = "response",
  newdata = dat_new
)

Specifying type = "response" returns predictions as probabilities on the original response scale rather than as log odds.
With two biomarkers, the model becomes:
\[
\operatorname{logit}(p_i)
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\beta_2x_{i2}.
\]

m2_binom <- glm(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  family = "binomial",
  data = binom_dat
)

We can then vary one biomarker while fixing the other at its minimum, mean or maximum value. Plotting these probability curves helps us understand the relative effects of the two biomarkers on the model predictions.

title: Part Three
text:
Residual Diagnostics
The observed residuals from a binary model are also discrete, so they do not behave like the continuous residuals from an ordinary linear regression. One option is to use binned residual plots, in which residuals are grouped across ranges of the fitted values. We look for systematic patterns and for bins that fall outside their expected error bounds.

library(performance)
library(see)

m2_binned_residuals <- binned_residuals(
  m2_binom,
  n_bins = 5,
  ci = 0.95,
  residuals = "deviance"
)

plot(m2_binned_residuals, show_dots = TRUE)

Simulation-based residual diagnostics, for example those available through DHARMa, provide another general approach for GLMs. A systematic rise and fall in the residuals may indicate an inadequately represented nonlinear relationship, although the appropriate response is not automatically to log-transform a predictor. We should consider whether a transformation, polynomial term, spline or interaction is supported by the scientific relationship.

title: Part Three
text:
Modelling Count Data
For a Poisson regression, the outcome is assumed to follow a Poisson distribution:
\[
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),
\]
where \(\lambda_i\) is both the expected count and, under the Poisson assumption, the variance:
\[
E(Y_i)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\lambda_i.
\]
The canonical link function is the natural logarithm:
\[
\log(\lambda_i)
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ik}.
\]
Using the inverse link gives:
\[
\lambda_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ik}),
\]
which ensures that the predicted mean count cannot be negative.

title: Part Three
section: An Example of Poisson Regression in R
text:
An Example of Poisson Regression in R
In the example presented in the slides, the observed count is modelled as a function of treatment and a continuous biomarker:

m1_pois <- glm(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  family = "poisson",
  data = pois_dat
)

summary(m1_pois)

The output again contains the coefficient estimates, standard errors, z-statistics, P-values, null deviance and residual deviance. Because the model uses a log link, exponentiating a coefficient gives a rate ratio or count ratio:
\[
\exp(\beta_j).
\]
For a continuous predictor, this is the multiplicative change in the expected count associated with a one-unit increase in the predictor, holding the other variables constant. For a categorical predictor, it compares the expected count with that of the reference category.
As with logistic regression, the difference between the null and residual deviances indicates how much the predictors improve fit relative to an intercept-only model. We should also examine residual diagnostics:

library(DHARMa)

sim_res <- simulateResiduals(m1_pois)
plot(sim_res)

DHARMa uses simulation to produce scaled residuals that can be assessed using familiar diagnostic plots and formal tests.

title: Part Three
text:
Overdispersion
The Poisson distribution is described using one parameter, \(\lambda\), which determines both its mean and variance. Real count data often have more variability than allowed by this assumption. This is called overdispersion.
If overdispersion is ignored, the model may underestimate the standard errors. Confidence intervals may then be too narrow and P-values too small. We can test dispersion using, for example, the testDispersion() function in DHARMa:

testDispersion(m1_pois)

A dispersion ratio greater than one indicates that the observed variability exceeds the variability expected under the fitted Poisson model. The magnitude, uncertainty and residual plots should be considered together rather than treating one as a universal pass-or-fail cut-off.
If the data are overdispersed, one alternative is negative binomial regression. The negative binomial model includes an additional parameter that allows the variance to exceed the mean:

library(MASS)

m2_pois <- glm.nb(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  data = pois_dat
)

summary(m2_pois)

title: Part Three
text:
Zero Inflation
Another feature of count data is an unexpectedly large number of zero-valued observations. For example, one patient group may have no detected metastases, while the positive counts in another group resemble a Poisson or negative binomial distribution.
Poisson and negative binomial models naturally allow zero counts and can accommodate some datasets containing many zeros. Switching to a negative binomial model may sometimes be sufficient when the apparent zero excess is associated with broader overdispersion.
When the data-generating process contains a separate source of structural zeros, we can consider a mixture model. A zero-inflated Poisson model combines a process that always produces a zero with a Poisson count process:

library(pscl)

m3_pois <- zeroinfl(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  data = pois_dat
)

summary(m3_pois)

The choice between Poisson, negative binomial, hurdle and zero-inflated models should be based on the assumed data-generating process as well as model diagnostics. A large number of observed zeros alone does not prove that a zero-inflated model is required.

title: Part Three
text:
Ordinal Logistic Regression
For an ordered outcome with \(K\) categories, an ordinal logistic regression models \(K-1\) cumulative log odds. The common proportional-odds formulation can be written as:
\[
\log\left[\frac{P(Y_i\leq j)}{P(Y_i>j)}\right]
=c_j-\mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol{\beta},
\qquad j=1,\ldots,K-1.
\]
The cut-points \(c_j\), sometimes shown as intercepts or thresholds, divide an underlying continuous tendency into the observed response categories. The linear predictor \(\mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol{\beta}\) shifts an observation along this underlying scale.
We fit one cumulative logistic comparison for each boundary between categories: category 1 versus categories above 1, categories 1-2 versus categories above 2, and so on. The cut-points differ between these comparisons, but the regression coefficients are assumed to remain the same. This is the proportional-odds assumption, also called the parallel-regression assumption.
The cut-points and regression coefficients are estimated simultaneously using maximum likelihood estimation. The residual variability relates partly to the fuzziness with which the underlying scale is separated into the observed response categories.

title: Part Three
text:
An Example in R
An ordinal logistic model can be fitted using polr() from the MASS package:

library(MASS)

ordinal_model <- polr(
  response ~ biomarker,
  data = ordinal_dat,
  Hess = TRUE
)

summary(ordinal_model)

In the slide example, the estimated biomarker coefficient is 1.185. With the sign convention used by polr(), a higher biomarker value is associated with greater odds of being in a higher response category. Exponentiating the coefficient gives the proportional odds ratio:
\[
\exp(1.185)\approx3.27.
\]
Thus, a one-unit increase in the biomarker multiplies the odds of being above rather than at or below any given category boundary by approximately 3.27, assuming proportional odds.
The intercepts labelled 1|2 and 2|3 are the estimated thresholds separating response category 1 from categories 2-3, and categories 1-2 from category 3. They locate the boundaries on the underlying logistic scale when the biomarker equals zero. They are not ordinary group means and are usually less scientifically interesting than the predictor coefficients.
The residual deviance measures model lack of fit and is mainly interpreted through comparison with a nested model. AIC can be compared across candidate models fitted to the same outcome data, including non-nested models, with lower values indicating a better trade-off between fit and complexity.

title: Part Three
text:
Model Diagnostics
The proportional-odds assumption can be assessed using, for example, Brant’s test:

library(brant)

brant(ordinal_model)

This examines whether the predictor coefficients can reasonably be treated as equal across the cumulative logits. As always, the test should be considered alongside graphical diagnostics, sample size and the practical magnitude of any departure.
We can also compare the predicted categories with the observed categories using a contingency table. Ideally, most observations fall along its diagonal:

predicted_category <- predict(ordinal_model, type = "class")
table(Actual = ordinal_dat$response, Predicted = predicted_category)

The example in the slides predicts categories one and three more successfully than the middle category. This may indicate that the middle category is difficult to separate using the available biomarker.
Surrogate residuals provide another way to examine ordinal regression models. The sure package can be used to generate residuals on a continuous scale:

library(sure)

ordinal_residuals <- resids(ordinal_model)
hist(ordinal_residuals)
qqnorm(ordinal_residuals)
qqline(ordinal_residuals)

We generally look for residuals centred around zero, with no systematic relationship with fitted values or predictors and no major departure from their expected distribution.

title: Part Three
text:
Modelling Unordered Categorical Data
Unordered categorical outcomes contain several categories without an inherent ranking. Examples could include alternative diagnoses or mutually exclusive choices.
With two outcome categories, a binomial probit model can be fitted in glm() using a probit link:

probit_model <- glm(
  outcome ~ x1 + x2,
  family = binomial(link = "probit"),
  data = choice_dat
)

For more than two unordered choices, a multinomial model is required. A multinomial probit model can, for example, be fitted using the MNP package:

library(MNP)
example(mnp)

title: Part Three
text:
Time-to-Event Data and Right Censoring
Participants or objects are followed until the event occurs or until the observation period ends. If the event has not occurred by the end of observation, the participant’s event time is right-censored. We know that the true event time is later than the observed follow-up time, but we do not know its exact value.
Right censoring may occur because:

a participant remains event-free at the end of the study;
a participant is lost to follow-up; or
a participant withdraws before experiencing the event.

Survival methods use the information available up to the censoring time rather than treating the censored participant as if the event occurred or discarding the participant completely. Standard methods usually assume that censoring is non-informative conditional on the variables in the model: participants censored at a given time should have a similar subsequent prognosis to comparable participants who remain under observation.

title: Part Three
text:
Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves
The Kaplan-Meier estimator provides a nonparametric estimate of the survival function:
\[
S(t)=P(T>t),
\]
the probability of remaining event-free beyond time \(t\). The estimate changes at observed event times and accounts for the number of participants still at risk.
We can create a survival object and fit a Kaplan-Meier curve using the survival package:

library(survival)

surv_object <- Surv(
  time = data$time,
  event = data$event
)

surv_km <- survfit(surv_object ~ 1)
plot(surv_km)

Here, event is normally coded as one when the event occurred and zero when the observation ∏was censored. The Kaplan-Meier curve moves downwards as events occur. A cumulative event or mortality curve, \(1-S(t)\), moves upwards towards one.
Kaplan-Meier curves can be used to compare groups visually. The log-rank test provides an overall comparison of the survival curves:

survdiff(
  Surv(time, event) ~ treatment,
  data = data
)

The null hypothesis is that the groups have the same survival experience over time. The log-rank test gives a test statistic and P-value, but it does not directly provide an effect estimate. An unadjusted Kaplan-Meier comparison also does not account for other predictors or potential confounders.

title: Part Three
text:
Cox Proportional-Hazards Regression
Cox regression models the relationship between a time-to-event outcome and one or more predictors. The hazard is the instantaneous event rate among individuals who have remained event-free up to time \(t\).
The Cox proportional-hazards model is:
\[
h(t\mid\mathbf{x})
=h_0(t)\exp(\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_kx_k),
\]
where \(h_0(t)\) is the baseline hazard at time \(t\). The method is semiparametric because the baseline hazard is left unspecified, while the predictor effects are described parametrically through the regression coefficients.
Exponentiating a coefficient gives a hazard ratio:
\[
HR_j=\exp(\beta_j).
\]
A hazard ratio above one indicates a higher instantaneous event rate, and a hazard ratio below one indicates a lower event rate, holding the other predictors constant. A hazard ratio is not a ratio of survival probabilities or a direct statement about the difference in median survival time.
We can fit a Cox model using coxph():

library(survival)
library(survminer)

m1_cox <- coxph(
  Surv(time, event) ~ treatment + age,
  data = data
)

summary(m1_cox)
ggforest(m1_cox, data = data)

The forest plot displays the estimated hazard ratios and their confidence intervals. This provides an effect estimate for treatment while adjusting for age.

title: Part Three
text:
The Proportional-Hazards Assumption
The Cox model assumes that the hazard ratio associated with a predictor remains constant over time. This is the proportional-hazards assumption. For example, if a treatment has a hazard ratio of 0.7, the model assumes that this relative effect is the same throughout follow-up, even though the baseline hazard itself may change.
We can assess this assumption using scaled Schoenfeld residuals and cox.zph():

proportionality_test <- cox.zph(m1_cox)
proportionality_test
plot(proportionality_test)

A systematic trend in the residual plot, or evidence from the test, may suggest that a predictor’s effect changes over time. Possible approaches include modelling an interaction with time, stratification or dividing the follow-up period into scientifically meaningful intervals.
As with the other models in this course, diagnostics and assumptions must be considered in relation to the study design and research question. Survival estimates depend on clearly defined time origins and events, adequate follow-up, appropriate handling of censoring and thoughtful selection of predictors.

title: Part Two
text:
NoteKey Takeaways




This second part of the course notebook will deal with relationships, linear regression models and multiple comparison. And, how regression models relate to t-tests and ANOVA.
Covariance, correlation and regression describe relationships between variables, but answer different questions. Covariance is a scale-dependent measure of how two variables vary together. Correlation is a standardised measure of association. And, regression models a dependent variable as a function of one or more predictors.
In linear regression, the coefficients describe the expected change in the dependent variable associated with a change in a predictor. Standard errors describe uncertainty in those estimates, while residual errors (or residuals) describe the differences between observed and predicted values.
Linear regression is subject to a number of assumptions. The validity of the data and model for the research question are perhaps the most important assumptions. Other considerations include linearity, independence of errors, homoscedasticity and the approximate normality of residual errors.
Ordinary least squares estimates the regression coefficients by minimising the sum of squared residuals. The same general linear-model framework connects regression, the t-test and analysis of variance (ANOVA).
Multiple regression can be used for estimation, hypothesis testing or prediction. Model-building decisions should follow the analytical purpose and should account for missingness, collinearity, interactions and the scale of the predictors.
ANOVA compares variation between group means given the variation within groups. A statistically significant overall test indicates that not all means are equal. Post-hoc comparisons are needed to identify which groups differ.

title: Part Two
text:
Covariance
Covariance is a scale-dependent measure of how two variables, such as \(X\) and \(Y\), vary together. For a sample of \(n\) paired observations, the sample covariance is: \[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}.
\]
The sign of the covariance describes the direction of the linear relationship:

\(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)<0\) indicates that larger values of one variable tend to occur with smaller values of the other.
\(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\approx0\) indicates approximately no linear relationship.
\(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)>0\) indicates that the variables tend to increase together.

Variance is a special case of covariance in which the two variables are the same:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,X).
\]
One limitation of covariance is that its magnitude depends on the units and scales of both variables. A covariance between weight in kilograms and height in centimetres cannot be directly compared with a covariance calculated using other units or variables.

title: Part Two
text:
Correlation
Correlation resolves this problem by standardising the covariance, i.e. Pearson’s correlation coefficient is calculated by dividing the covariance by the standard deviations of the two variables:
\[
r_{xy}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{s_xs_y}.
\]
The resulting coefficient r ranges from -1 to 1. A value close to -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship, a value close to 1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship, and a value close to zero indicates little or no linear relationship.
Pearson’s correlation coefficient is suitable for linear relationships. For a monotonic relationship that may be nonlinear, we can instead use a rank-based measure such as Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient or Kendall’s tau. A monotonic relationship consistently moves in one direction: as one variable increases, the other either consistently increases or consistently decreases. Kendall’s tau compares concordant and discordant pairs and can be more robust than Spearman’s correlation in some settings.
It is important to plot the paired data before interpreting a correlation coefficient. A single coefficient can conceal nonlinear relationships, clusters, influential observations and other important features of the data. Also remember that correlation does not establish causation.

title: Part Two
text:
From Association to Regression
Linear regression models describe the relationship between a dependent variable, also called an outcome or response \(Y\), and one or more independent variables or predictors \(X\):
\[
Y_i=f(X_i,\boldsymbol{\beta})+\varepsilon_i.
\]
For a simple linear regression, this becomes:
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.
\]
The intercept \(\beta_0\) describes the expected value of \(Y\) when \(X=0\). The slope \(\beta_1\) describes the expected change in \(Y\) associated with a one-unit increase in \(X\). The error term \(\varepsilon_i\) represents the part of the observation that is not explained by the deterministic component of the model.
We usually assign the dependent variable to the effect or outcome that we want to study. The independent variables are then the exposures, treatments, characteristics or predictors that may explain variation in that outcome. Regression can therefore be used to estimate relationships in a sample and, subject to the study design and assumptions, make inferences about a population.

title: Part Two
text:
A Simple Regression Model
We can use Galton’s height data to ask the following research question:
To what degree does parents’ average height explain variability in the height of their adult children?
The corresponding simple regression model is therefore:
\[
\widehat{\text{child height}}=\beta_0+\beta_1\times\text{parent height}.
\]
Here, \(\widehat{\text{child height}}\) is the predicted or expected child height given the parents’ average height. The intercept \(\beta_0\) is the predicted height of the adult child when parent height is zero. This interpetation is of course not very meaningful because a parent height of zero is impossible. Instead, we can make the intercept more useful by centering parent height around a relevant reference value, such as its sample mean. The intercept would then represent the expected child height for parents of average height.
The slope \(\beta_1\) is the expected change in child height associated with a one-unit increase in parent height. In the example presented in the slides, the estimated slope is approximately 0.52. This means that for every additional inch in parents’ average height, the child’s expected adult height increases by approximately 0.52 inches.
In R, we can fit the model using the linear model function, lm():

# Importing the data
height_galt <- read.csv("Height_dat_Galton1886.csv")

# Formatting the data
library(dplyr)

            .groups = 'drop')

height_df <- height_tbl %>% as.data.frame()

# Defining an fitting the linear regression model:
model_fit <- lm(child_height ~ parent_height, data = height_df)

The residual for observation \(i\) is the difference between the observed and fitted values:
\[
e_i=y_i-\widehat{y}_i.
\]
Residuals are central to regression diagnostics because they describe the part of the data that the model has not explained.

title: Part Two
text:
Assumptions of Linear Regression
Much is written on the assumptions of linear regression and how these should be investigated to determine if they are satisfied. I think Gelman and Hill (Gelman and Hill (2007)) provides an excellent summary where they order the assumptions and considerations for linear regression approximately as follows: 1. Validity: the analysed data maps to the research question. 2. Additivity and linearity: the relationship between the predictors and outcome is additive and linear. 3. Independence of errors: the residual errors are independent, conditional on the predictors included in the model. 4. Homoscedasticity: the residual errors have approximately constant variance across the fitted values. 5. Normality: the residual errors are approximately normally distributed.
This ordering matters. A perfectly normal residual distribution cannot rescue a model based on an invalid outcome measure or a study design that does not address the research question. Normality is often the least important of these assumptions for estimating the regression coefficients (and perhaps the most misunderstood?), although substantial departures can affect small-sample inference and prediction intervals. A common misconception is that linear models require the dependent data to be normally distributed, this is not the case. We are interested in the approximate normality of the residual errors meaning the residuals are approximately symmetric around zero.
Validity concerns what the data actually represent. In the height example, we should ask when the children’s height was measured, whether the measurements represent adult height, how parent height was defined and whether the sampled families represent the population to which we want to generalise.
Linearity can first be assessed by plotting the outcome against the predictor. If the relationship is clearly nonlinear, possible solutions include transforming a variable, introducing polynomial or spline terms, or using another model that represents the scientific relationship more appropriately. Adding terms merely to improve a diagnostic plot, without considering the research question, is not a sufficient modelling strategy.
The remaining assumptions mainly concern the residual error structure. We can investigate our assumptions using the standard diagnostic plots produced by plot(model_fit) in R:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_fit)







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Residuals versus fitted values: used to look for nonlinearity and non-constant variance. Ideally, the residuals form an approximately random band around zero.
Normal Q-Q Residual plot: compares the standardised residuals with the theoretical quantiles of a normal distribution. Departures in the tails may indicate skewness, heavy tailedness or unusual observations.
Scale-location plot: displays the spread of the root standardised residuals across fitted values and helps assess homoscedasticity.
Residuals versus leverage: helps identify observations that may have a large influence on the fitted coefficients. Cook’s distance combines residual size and leverage as an indicator of influence.

These plots are diagnostic tools, not pass-or-fail tests. An observation with high leverage has an unusual predictor value. It becomes particularly influential when it also has a substantial residual. Influential observations should be investigated further, they should not be removed automatically.

title: Part Two
text:
Confidence Intervals and Prediction Intervals
Regression can be used to estimate the mean outcome at a predictor value or to predict a future observation. These require different intervals.
A confidence interval describes uncertainty in the estimated conditional mean. Under repeated sampling, 95% of intervals constructed in the same way would contain the true conditional population mean. The interval is usually narrowest near predictor values where the data provide the most information.
A prediction interval describes uncertainty for a future individual observation. It includes both uncertainty in the estimated mean and the residual variation between observations. It is therefore wider than the corresponding confidence interval.

# Confidence interval for the conditional mean
modelprediction_ci <- predict(model_fit, newdata = height_df,
        interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)

# Prediction interval for a future observation
modelprediction_pi <- predict(model_fit, newdata = height_df,
        interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)

plot_dat <- data.frame(modelprediction_ci, modelprediction_pi, height_df)

library(ggplot2)

# plot confidence intervals
ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x=parent_height, y=child_height)) + 
    geom_point(colour = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lwr), linewidth = 0.5, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = upr), linewidth = 0.5, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, fill = "red", color = NULL), alpha = 0.15) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  ggtitle("95% Confidence Interval") +
  xlab("Parent height [inches]") +
  ylab("Child height [inches]")







# plot prediction intervals
